sources.title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI (AI Engineer Miami keynote, day-1 livestream segment)
sources.note: Segment file lines 119-781 cover the whole keynote (intro to applause); the rest of the segment is the next panel, not Dex. Auto-captions, no timestamps.

sources.title: AI Engineer Miami 2026 event page
sources.note: Talk abstract: large orgs, discrete research and planning steps, control flow instead of prompting, PR slop.

sources.title: Full-day transcript 6IxSbMhT7v4.txt
sources.note: Not opened. The keynote ended inside the segment file, so reading further was unnecessary.

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have an instruction budget
cards.claim: Every prompt, CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tool set and MCP draws on one limited budget of instructions the model can follow.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites Kyle's CLAUDE.md post: frontier models follow about 150-200 instructions before half-attending to all; number inflated a year on but a budget still exists.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md length trim (W1); count instructions across CLAUDE.md plus skills plus phase routine

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 85 instructions plus your cloudmd plus your system prompt plus your tools
cards.claim: A single mega-prompt of 85 instructions on top of CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tools and MCP is very unlikely to get adherence, and the plan step was skipped about half the time.
cards.evidence_detail: Customer onboarding: experts got great results, teammates did not; without the 'magic words' the model skipped the Q&A step roughly 50% of the time.
cards.landing: Phase routine in ship plan section 0: check how many instructions it carries and whether any step can silently be skipped

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you build a tool that requires hours of training, like go fix the tool
cards.claim: If a workflow only works when the user says magic words, the tool is at fault, not the user.
cards.evidence_detail: Seven hours of training for three steps; some users got bad plans for lack of one repeated sentence.
cards.landing: Phase routine should not depend on the agent being told a particular phrase; cold-resume trial P1

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't use prompts for control flow if you can use control flow for control flow
cards.claim: Sequencing, branching and step selection belong in code (switch and if statements) around small prompts, not in one prompt that describes the workflow.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as the lesson after splitting create_plan; also a classify-then-smaller-instruction-module example from customer support bots; says a smaller, dumber model may then suffice.
cards.landing: Workflow scripts (W5) and a phase driver instead of prose in ship plan section 0

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: now they're all under 40 instructions
cards.claim: The 85-instruction create_plan prompt was split into design, structure and plan prompts, each under 40 instructions.
cards.evidence_detail: Before/after instruction counts only; no adherence rate given.
cards.landing: Skills split: keep each skill or agent prompt under about 40 instructions

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: hide the ticket from the researcher programmatically
cards.claim: Research stays objective if one context turns the ticket into questions and a second context, never shown the ticket, answers only the questions.
cards.evidence_detail: Bad research (given the ticket) carries opinions steered toward the model's first-picked solution; can be done with plain prompting and a workflow, same as deep-research systems.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial and verifier design: refuters/researchers get questions, not the proposed answer; Workflow script step

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a good research is mostly facts, but a bad research will have opinions
cards.claim: Research output should be a compressed, objective snapshot of how the code works today, with no opinions or implementation planning.
cards.evidence_detail: Lazy 'research, I have to do this' prompts versus ticket-derived questions such as how endpoints are registered.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store entries for verified diagnoses: facts only, separate from proposals

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Don't read the plans, just read the code.
cards.claim: Reading a long plan is not leverage because a thousand-line plan costs about as much reading as the thousand lines of code, and the code must be read anyway; review the code, not the plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Reverses his November 2025 'you have to read the plan' advice; order-of-magnitude equivalence of plan and code length.
cards.landing: Owner review of draft PR bodies and plan docs: where human reading effort goes

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Please read the code.
cards.claim: Not reading the code (lights-off software factory) failed over about six months and forced ripping out large parts of the system; he advises reading every line and aiming for 2-3x rather than 10x.
cards.evidence_detail: Own six-month experience; warns of three weeks of re-onboarding downtime if nobody has read the code for three months.
cards.landing: Owner view and reviewer role: keep a human code-read step on the critical paths (money, outbox, lifecycle)

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: what's the right speed you can go
cards.claim: Agent swarms and maximal token spend are the wrong bottleneck; the question is a sustainable speed, since 10x output thrown away in six months is burned time and money.
cards.evidence_detail: Contrasts last year's 'spend as many tokens as possible' with this year's rate question; says he is iffy on agent swarms.
cards.landing: Ship plan pacing; effort routing (token smarter, not harder)

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: anyone here the rag pipeline?
cards.claim: Context engineering has two reads: put better information in the window, and put better instructions in it; the second is the one people neglect.
cards.evidence_detail: Framing remark before the instruction-budget argument.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md and knowledge-store design: audit instructions, not only facts

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: over about 100,000 tokens
cards.claim: The dumb zone begins around 100,000 tokens for a Claude model (the GPT figure differs), so more context past that degrades results.
cards.evidence_detail: Number quoted from memory, attributed to the earlier dumb-zone talk; he flags the GPT threshold as different.
cards.landing: One-phase-per-session rule; compaction trigger around 100k tokens

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: same amount of attention spread out over more instructions is not going to fix this
cards.claim: A bigger context window does not fix instruction overload; attention is spread thinner over more instructions.
cards.evidence_detail: Response to the idea that more context capacity removes the budget.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim rationale

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: difference between 99% and 97% is a 27% gap
cards.claim: In long-horizon agentic tasks small per-step reliability gains compound, so by turn 20 a 99% versus 97% step reliability is a 27% gap.
cards.evidence_detail: Arithmetic of compounding over 20 turns, used to justify context engineering past the naive-prompting frontier.
cards.landing: Why per-step verification and short sessions matter

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: won't this just get bitter lessened?
cards.claim: Context engineering will be partly obsoleted by each new model but keeps you 1-10% ahead of naive prompting; it can let a small cheap model do a bigger model's work.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites Dan Shipper's 'surfing the models' and Swix's view that the bitter lesson will win eventually; example: get GPT-OSS to do GPT-5-high work.
cards.landing: Decision to invest in saved workflows versus waiting for models; cheaper model routing

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Design is where we're going. Structure is how we get there.
cards.claim: Planning is split into a design discussion (current state, desired end state, patterns to follow, open questions; about 200 lines) and a structure outline (phases and checkpoints), mapping to design review and sprint planning.
cards.evidence_detail: Used internally and with customers; QRSPI = questions, research, design, structure outline, plan, worktree, implement, pull request.
cards.landing: Phase routine and draft-PR 'Plan @ sha' body: add a short design/outline artifact before the plan

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: brain surgery on the agent before it actually goes and slops out
cards.claim: The design doc is the cheap place to steer the agent: have it brain-dump its understanding and the patterns it found, and correct bad-pattern choices before any code exists.
cards.evidence_detail: Legacy codebases have six ways to do everything; the human picks the right one at the design step.
cards.landing: Decisions journal in the draft PR; owner checkpoint after design

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can't RL a model on architecture
cards.claim: Humans must stay in the loop at design because bad architecture has a cost measured in months and years, so it cannot be trained against five-minute test cycles.
cards.evidence_detail: Reason given for keeping the human at the design step; cites the Brooks 'design concept' idea via Matt Pocock.
cards.landing: Which phases require an owner decision versus verifier approval

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models just absolutely freaking love these horizontal plans
cards.claim: Models plan by layer (database, services, API, front end) producing 1200 lines before anything is checked; the outline step should force vertical slices with a check after each small increment.
cards.evidence_detail: Large debug surface when something breaks; remedy is a human re-steer at the structure outline ('build it the way you would have as an engineer').
cards.landing: Phase sizing and per-slice fail-before/pass-after checks in the reviewer routine

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you just bot check it
cards.claim: The line-by-line plan is for the agent, not for humans; reviewers read the high-level documents and the code, and only spot-check the plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Higher-order documents give more leverage: the human reads less and the model uses fewer tokens.
cards.landing: Owner one-page view built from design/outline, not the full plan

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you don't trust what the model's going to do
cards.claim: The high-level documents can be expanded on demand: if the outline is not trusted, ask the model to add detail.
cards.evidence_detail: Docs start high level and are plain markdown.
cards.landing: Progressive-disclosure plan artifacts in the draft PR

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Brooks had this idea of this thing that is never written down
cards.claim: Writing the shared understanding of the design into a 200-line markdown artifact gives alignment with the agent and with teammates, and shortens code review.
cards.evidence_detail: Alignment work not worth doing by hand in a Google doc becomes worth it when AI drafts it; compresses code-review cycles; two-hour coding tasks used to take two days because of alignment.
cards.landing: Knowledge store and decisions journal: externalise the design concept

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're not going to go 2x faster
cards.claim: Using AI only for coding speeds you up modestly; the larger gain comes from using it for planning and team alignment, which cuts rework and review time.
cards.evidence_detail: Large-org experience (hundreds of engineers); no numbers.
cards.landing: Where the harness spends agent effort: plan and review rather than only implementation

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Raise your hand if you use this prompt.
cards.claim: A methodology that works for an expert often fails when handed to a team, so rollout needs time spent watching real users struggle with it.
cards.evidence_detail: Thousands of engineers and companies of all sizes since October; 'hundreds of hours' watching users; RPI use claimed at Uber and Block.
cards.landing: P1 cold-resume trial design: test the routine with an agent other than the author

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: There is no magic prompt.
cards.claim: The QRSPI prompts are deliberately unpublished; the point is to learn instruction budgeting, and if results are poor, break the three prompts into about eight smaller workflows.
cards.evidence_detail: Derivation left as an exercise; open-source HumanLayer prompts are the starting point.
cards.landing: Skill and workflow library: many small prompts, each owned and tested

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how do we evaluate that?
cards.claim: Teams adopting a prompting system need to know what is working and why, and how to evaluate changes to the prompts; he offers no answer in this talk and points to a separate adoption talk (process, defensible metric, one person shipping non-slop).
cards.evidence_detail: Open problem stated; also says he has no answer yet on testing and verification.
cards.landing: Measurement pipeline (skipped by the harness review): mark as re-opening

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Repeat the most important instruction at the very end of the prompt
cards.claim: A standard prompting rule: repeat the most important instruction at both the start and the end of the prompt.
cards.evidence_detail: Cited as what the 'magic words' implement; not claimed as a fix.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md structure: place critical invariants at top and end

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: what is PR slop, where does it come from, and how to combat it
cards.claim: The talk abstract promises a view on what PR slop is, where it comes from and how to combat it, but the delivered keynote does not cover it.
cards.evidence_detail: Event-page abstract only; absent from the transcript read.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; check later talks or posts for the PR-slop argument

gaps: Full-day transcript (6IxSbMhT7v4.txt) not opened; the keynote was complete inside the segment file (lines 119-781).
Auto-captions have no timestamps; the 'PR slop' topic from the abstract was not delivered in the transcript.
No numbers measured in the talk beyond quoted figures (150-200 instruction budget, 85 vs 40 instructions, 100k tokens, 99% vs 97%); none are from an experiment.
The segment file also begins with the end of Dax Raad's talk and ends in a CodeRabbit panel; neither was carded (not Dex).
